title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
claim: Our bounds are tighter than prior bounds and grow far less as architecture width increases, capturing the benefit of sparsity.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bar chart, left-to-right, bars grouped by method and colored by width
description: A single wide grouped bar chart comparing generalization bounds on a log-2 scale (y-axis, 0 to 5). The x-axis has five groups: Graf et al. 2022, Ledent et al. 2025 without loss-aug, Ledent et al. 2025 with loss-aug, Ours without loss-aug, and Ours with loss-aug. Each group has four bars colored by network width: blue for 400, orange for 600, red for 800 and teal for 1000. A legend sits at top right. The Graf et al. bars are tallest, about 4.3 to 5.1, and rise steeply with width. The Ledent et al. bars are lower, and the Ours bars are lowest and nearly flat across widths. The eye goes first to the tall Graf bars on the left, then to the short Ours bars on the right.
caption: Generalization bounds evaluated for convolutional neural networks with different fully-connected layer widths. All results have negligible logarithmic terms truncated. Logarithmic terms involving product of weight norms across all layers are expressed as $\sqrt{L}$ (as in $\widetilde O$-notation). For the exact formulas of evaluated bounds, we refer readers to Table [ref].
abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.
